sections.h2: What should a Princeton seller handle before closing?
sections.html:
Most Princeton sellers need three items: a smoke and carbon monoxide alarm certificate from the Bureau of Fire Safety, a construction records clearance from the Building Department, and a sewer affidavit about sump pumps and roof drains. Each has its own fee and lead time, so start them as soon as a contract is signed.

Princeton is a single municipality in Mercer County, formed when the borough and township merged on January 1, 2013. Whether you list with an agent, sell privately or take an as-is cash offer, those three items and the deed recorded in Trenton apply to the house.

Princeton had an estimated 31,469 residents in mid-2025 and 9,300 households. Owners live in 55.4 percent of homes. The median owned home is valued at $1,050,600, median gross rent is $2,636 and median household income is $192,079.

A median value above $1,050,000 puts many Princeton sales into the state's highest fee brackets, covered below. Ask for recent sold prices on your own street instead of leaning on the citywide figure. Ask your agent how the academic calendar affects showing and offer timing on your street, since Princeton University shapes the local market.

Listing photos and descriptions that name a school should match the district's current attendance zones. Check with the district office before you repeat an assignment in marketing copy.

Princeton's ZIP codes run from 08540 to 08544, with 08542 mostly covering the old borough. Cedar Grove, Port Mercer, Princeton Basin and Jugtown are unincorporated communities that keep their own identities within the larger municipality, so make sure your listing, deed and tax records all use the correct address and block and lot.

Buyers often weigh the rail link to Princeton Junction, where trains join Amtrak's Northeast Corridor and NJ Transit service toward Manhattan, and the public school system. Mention both accurately in your listing, and keep any claim about school assignment consistent with the district's own information.

sections.h2: The three Princeton seller requirements and their costs
sections.html:
Fees below may change, so confirm with each office when you apply.

Princeton seller requirements and fees
RequirementOfficeFee
Smoke and carbon monoxide certificate, initial inspectionBureau of Fire Safety$50 per unit, one reinspection included
Added reinspectionBureau of Fire Safety$50 per unit
Construction records clearanceBuilding Department$35, $70 or $125 by lead time
Sewer Affidavit of ComplianceSewer Operating Committee$20, or $50 with an inspection

The construction records clearance is $35 when requested 11 to 20 business days before closing, $70 at 6 to 10 business days out, and $125 at 1 to 5 business days out. Pay by check to "Princeton" or with exact cash.

The sewer affidavit with the Princeton Sewer Operating Committee covers sump pumps, roof drains and similar drains. An inspection is available for $50 if the owner asks for one, and the certification takes 7 to 10 business days.

The fire certificate fee depends on timing. It is $45 per unit when the application is completed more than 10 days before closing, $90 per unit between 4 and 10 days before, and $161 per unit with less than 4 days left. Filing early saves $116 per unit.

If a building will be torn down or renovated with no change in occupancy, the Bureau of Fire Safety can provide a letter stating that no alarm certificate is required.

sections.h2: State fees on a high-value Princeton sale
sections.html:
The seller pays the realty transfer fee. On sales above $350,000 the Division of Taxation schedule reaches $5.80 per $500 between $850,000 and $1,000,000 and $6.05 per $500 above $1,000,000.

A second charge, the Graduated Percent Fee, applies to residential deeds with consideration above $1,000,000. It is 1% of total consideration up to $2,000,000, 2% above that to $2,500,000, 2.5% to $3,000,000, 3% to $3,500,000 and 3.5% beyond. Form RTF-1EE is attached to every deed over $1,000,000.

Deeds go to the Mercer County Clerk's Office at 209 South Broad Street in Trenton. Deeds recorded after July 10, 2025 with consideration over $1,000,000 fall under the revised state fee.

sections.h2: How to line up the Princeton paperwork
sections.html:
The three city items run on separate clocks, so sequence them. Request the construction records clearance first, because the $35 rate needs 11 to 20 business days and the sewer certification takes 7 to 10 business days. Complete the fire safety application more than 10 days before closing to pay $45 per unit instead of $90 or $161.

Gather the sewer questions early: where the sump pumps and roof drains discharge, and whether you want the optional $50 inspection. If a house will be rebuilt, ask the Building Department what the records clearance covers before you agree to a closing date.

Your closing agent normally submits the deed and state affidavits to the Mercer County Clerk. Confirm with them whether the higher state fees apply at your price, and ask for the closing statement draft early so nothing about the transfer fee or the Graduated Percent Fee surprises you at the table. Keep receipts for the fire, records and sewer fees in one folder, since the buyer's side may ask to see each certificate before funds are released.

sections.h2: Which sale route fits a Princeton homeowner?
sections.html:
A broker listing gives you exposure to buyers who value the schools and the rail link, but it adds staging, showings and a lender's appraisal. A private sale saves a commission and leaves you to arrange the three city items yourself.

A cash buyer purchasing as-is can shorten the calendar, although the fire certificate, records clearance and sewer affidavit still need to be in hand. Compare offers by your net after fees, repairs and carrying costs.

On a high-priced house the state fees are a large line item, so ask each buyer who pays what and request a written estimate from your closing agent. A cash sale does skip the lender's appraisal and a long list of buyer repair requests, which can matter when a closing date is fixed. For a teardown or major rebuild, a buyer will usually want the construction records clearance in hand early, so settle who orders it when you sign the contract.

faqs.q: What does Princeton require before I sell my house?
faqs.a: Most sellers need a smoke and carbon monoxide certificate from the Bureau of Fire Safety, a construction records clearance from the Building Department and a sewer affidavit. Each is filed separately with its own fee, so contact all three offices once a closing date exists.

faqs.q: How much does the Princeton fire safety certificate cost?
faqs.a: The initial inspection is $50 per unit with one reinspection included. The certificate itself costs $45 per unit if you apply more than 10 days before closing, $90 between 4 and 10 days and $161 with less than 4 days left.

faqs.q: How long does the Princeton construction records clearance take?
faqs.a: Request it 11 to 20 business days before closing for $35. The fee rises to $70 at 6 to 10 business days and $125 at 1 to 5 business days, so earlier requests cost less.

faqs.q: Are there extra state fees on a Princeton sale above one million dollars?
faqs.a: Yes. The seller owes the Graduated Percent Fee, which starts at 1% of total consideration for deeds above $1,000,000, in addition to the realty transfer fee. Form RTF-1EE is attached to the deed.

faqs.q: Where is a Princeton deed recorded?
faqs.a: With the Mercer County Clerk, 209 South Broad Street, Trenton. Your closing agent normally submits the deed and the state affidavits there.
